title: Urbanization Amplifies Regional Precipitation Contrasts but not Urban‐Core Precipitation Extremes
content:
Abstract

Urbanization is often assumed to intensify precipitation and concentrate flood-relevant extremes in city centers, yet clear observational evidence remains limited. Here, we analyze warm-season sub-daily precipitation during 2000–2024 across 20 urban agglomerations and 61 representative cities in China, partitioning built-up areas into three urban-intensity zones based on impervious surface fraction. Total precipitation generally increases more rapidly in urban areas than in nearby non-urban reference regions, with about 75% of urban agglomerations showing faster urban wetting. However, this enhancement is primarily driven by light-to-moderate precipitation, for which urbanization effects strengthen systematically from weakly to highly urbanized zones. Quantitatively, urban-intensity sensitivity is positive for non-extreme precipitation, with urbanization effects increasing by about 0.1–0.7 mm yr−1 for each 10% increase in impervious surface fraction, but it becomes negative for extremes, decreasing on average by about 0.5–1.1 mm yr−1. Accordingly, only 20%–25% of urban agglomerations show stronger amplification of extreme precipitation in highly urbanized zones, whereas roughly one-third show weaker or negative urbanization effects in these zones. These patterns are consistent at the city scale, are more evident at hourly than daily resolution, and are strongest in humid regions. Our results show that stronger urbanization amplifies regional precipitation contrasts but does not systematically amplify precipitation extremes in urban cores, challenging a common assumption in urban flood-risk assessment and emphasizing the need to distinguish general urban wetting from changes in short-duration hazardous rainfall.
